title: The Promised Seed and the Departure
setting: The highest hill of Paradise, where Michael tells Adam the rest of history, then the bower and the eastern gate
summary: Michael tells Adam the rest of history: Babel, Abraham, Moses and the Law, the kings of Israel, and the coming of the Messiah, who will defeat Satan by obedience and suffering rather than by force. Adam rejoices that so much good will come out of his sin, and learns that a ‘paradise within’ can replace the one he is losing. Eve wakes comforted by a dream, and Michael leads them out of Eden hand in hand into the world.

sections.title: After the Flood: Nimrod and Babel
sections.note: Seeing Adam’s sight fail, Michael switches from visions to narration. The new race lives in peace until a proud tyrant claims dominion over his brothers and builds a tower to reach Heaven, and God scatters the builders by confounding their tongues.

sections.title: Tyranny and lost liberty
sections.note: Adam protests that God gave man rule over beasts, not over other men. Michael agrees, but explains that since the Fall inner passions usurp reason, and those who lose inward freedom are justly handed over to outward tyrants.

sections.title: The call of Abraham
sections.note: God chooses one faithful man, brought up among idol-worshippers, and calls him to a land he will be shown. Michael points out the borders of Canaan and reveals that Abraham’s seed is the Deliverer who will bruise the Serpent’s head.

sections.title: Egypt and the Exodus
sections.note: Abraham’s descendants go down into Egypt, multiply, and are enslaved. Moses and Aaron bring ten plagues on Pharaoh, the sea parts to let Israel through and closes on his army, and God leads them the long way through the desert.

sections.title: Sinai, the tabernacle and Canaan
sections.note: God gives the Law from Sinai in thunder, and the people ask for Moses as go-between, a figure of a greater Mediator to come. God dwells among them in the tabernacle, and they win the promised land, the sun standing still for Joshua.

sections.title: Adam asks why so many laws
sections.note: Adam rejoices to learn of Abraham’s seed, but wonders how God can live among people who need so many laws, since many laws imply many sins.

sections.title: Law and grace
sections.note: Michael explains that the Law exists to show people their sin and their need for a better sacrifice. It is a schoolmaster leading from shadow to truth, which is why Joshua, whose name is Jesus, and not Moses, leads the people into Canaan.

sections.title: Kings, exile and the Messiah’s birth
sections.note: Israel lives under judges and then kings, and David is promised an everlasting throne. After idolatry, exile in Babylon and strife among the priests, the true King is born of a virgin and announced by a star and by angels.

sections.title: Adam hails the Virgin Mother
sections.note: Adam, overjoyed, finally understands why the Deliverer is called the seed of the Woman. He asks eagerly where and when the duel with the Serpent will be fought.

sections.title: How the Serpent is truly defeated
sections.note: Michael warns him not to imagine a duel: the Son will conquer by fulfilling the law in obedience and love, dying on the cross for mankind, and rising on the third day. He will ascend in triumph and return at the end to judge the world and make the whole earth a paradise.

sections.title: O Goodness infinite
sections.note: Adam marvels that all this good will come from evil, and wonders whether to repent his sin or rejoice in it. Then he asks what will become of the faithful left behind when their Deliverer returns to Heaven.

sections.title: The Spirit, the wolves and the end of time
sections.note: Michael says the Spirit will guide and arm believers, but after the apostles ‘grievous wolves’ will turn religion into a tool of wealth and power and force consciences. The world will go on groaning until the Son returns to dissolve it and raise new heavens and a new earth.

sections.title: Adam’s lesson
sections.note: Adam says he has learned the sum: to obey, to love God with fear, and to trust that God accomplishes great things by small and weak ones. Suffering for truth is the highest fortitude, and he names his Redeemer.

sections.title: A paradise within
sections.note: Michael tells him that this is the sum of wisdom; if he adds deeds, faith, patience and above all love, he will have ‘a Paradise within thee, happier far.’ The flaming sword is waving, and Adam must wake Eve and share the promise with her.

sections.title: Eve’s last words
sections.note: Eve, woken by a hopeful dream, tells Adam that wherever he is will be Paradise to her. Her consolation is that the Promised Seed will come through her, who lost all.

sections.title: The expulsion
sections.note: The cherubim glide down like evening mist, the sword blazing before them, and Michael takes the lingering pair by the hand and leads them down to the plain. They look back once, shed a few tears, and walk out hand in hand into the world.

glosses.note: Slows down or stops to rest; short for ‘abates.’
Nimrod, called ‘a mighty hunter before the Lord’ in Genesis 10; Milton makes his game men rather than beasts.

glosses.word: from rebellion shall derive his name
glosses.note: Nimrod’s name was linked to the Hebrew marad, ‘to rebel.’
A whirlpool of pitch; Genesis says the builders of Babel used slime (bitumen) for mortar.
Erase, wipe out.
Babel, which Genesis links to the Hebrew balal, ‘to confuse.’
Separate; liberty and reason have no existence apart from each other.
Ham, who saw his drunken father Noah naked; Noah cursed Ham’s son Canaan to be a ‘servant of servants’ (Genesis 9).
Specially chosen, God’s own; from the biblical ‘a peculiar people.’
Abraham’s home city in Mesopotamia; Haran was his first stop on the way to Canaan.
Shechem, where Abraham first camped in Canaan, near the oak (or plain) of Moreh.
Hamath in Syria, the northern limit of the promised land; the ‘Desart south’ is the Wilderness of Zin.
The Jordan, believed to spring from two sources named Jor and Dan.
A peak of the Hermon range, beyond the Jordan.
Later, succeeding: the new Pharaoh ‘which knew not Joseph’ (Exodus 1).
Murrain, a deadly plague of cattle.
Boils and blisters; ‘emboss’ means to swell with lumps.
Pharaoh, called ‘the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers’ in Ezekiel 29.
Crack or shatter; Exodus says God ‘took off their chariot wheels.’
The seven-branched lampstand of the tabernacle was read as a figure of the seven planets moving through the zodiac.
Aijalon, the valley over which the moon stood still while Joshua defeated the Amorites at Gibeon (Joshua 10).
Depravity, corruption.
‘Jesus’ is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, so Joshua leading Israel into Canaan prefigures Christ.
To the head (Latin caput), and also deadly, fatal: a pun on the Serpent’s bruised head.
Heal, restore.
Satisfied, paid in full.
Flowing; Milton held that baptism should be in running water.
Paul’s warning in Acts 20:29; Milton aims it at a worldly, power-seeking clergy.
Breathing space, relief; the ‘times of refreshing’ of Acts 3:19.
Scorched, burnt dry.

famous.why: ‘Man over men he made not lord’: Milton’s republican politics put into the mouth of the first man.
Adam’s ‘O Goodness infinite’ is the poem’s statement of the ‘fortunate fall,’ the idea that the Fall made possible a greater good.
Michael’s promise of ‘a Paradise within thee, happier far’ gives the poem its final consolation.
Eve’s ‘with thee to go, is to stay here’ turns the loss of a place into a vow of love.
The closing lines, quiet and open-ended, among the most admired endings in English poetry.

themes: Good is brought out of evil: the Fall becomes the occasion for redemption.
True liberty depends on reason ruling within; inner slavery invites outer tyranny.
History is read as a pattern of figures pointing to the Redeemer.
A lost place is replaced by an inner paradise of faith, obedience and love.
art: Michael leading Adam and Eve by the hand down from the eastern gate, the flaming sword blazing behind them, as the pair look back toward Paradise.
